phases.name: RRG Season
phases.goal: Send 5.12 at RRG or Obed. Rebuild the aerobic forearm base from scratch.

phases.name: Sharpen
phases.goal: Run an honest 5K off ~12 weeks of base. Expect 19:30–20:30 — it is regaining, not building from scratch.

phases.name: Deep Winter
phases.goal: V10 indoors. V11 if the winter goes perfectly.

phases.name: Run Block
phases.goal: Sub-18:30 by mid-July, with 17:56 live in the autumn. You have run it before.

phases.name: Turn
phases.goal: Walk into fall 2027 with the engine for 5.13.

ex: All four fingers on the edge, middle knuckles bent to about 90 degrees, fingertips flat and thumb off. The default hangboard grip. If the knuckles collapse flat you have drifted into an open hand; if they hyperextend you are full-crimping.
Index, middle and ring finger only, hanging open and relaxed with the knuckles soft. Little finger stays off the edge. No thumb.
Middle, ring and little finger only, open hand. Feels much harder than the front three because the little finger carries load it is not used to — build into it slowly.

A dead hang on ONE arm, not a pull-up. Stand one foot in a band hung beside the board, or run a cord over a pulley to a counterweight, taking off just enough weight to hold 8 to 10 seconds. Remove assistance over months.
Consciously tense the forearm and set the wrist BEFORE you take any load, then grip. The whole point is doing it in the right order until it happens without thinking.
All three of the above back to back — fingers forward, fingers back, then fingers out to the sides. 30 seconds each.
Wrist isometric, 4 directions vs other hand
Push the working wrist against your other hand and hold, resisting in each of four directions: up, down, and each side. Nothing moves.
On all fours, palms flat, fingers pointing forward. Rock weight gently over the hands and back. Search "quadruped wrist rock".
Same position but with the fingers pointing back toward your knees. Rock gently — this one is a strong stretch, so keep it well short of pain.
Palms flat, fingers pointing out to the sides. Rock side to side over the hands.
Wrist isometric, 4 directions vs other hand
Push the working wrist against your other hand and hold, resisting in each of four directions: up, down, and each side. Nothing moves.
Hold a hammer or wrench near the end of the handle, elbow tucked at 90 degrees, and rotate the palm up then down. The long handle is what makes it hard.
Hand into a bucket of rice (or squeeze a ball), opening and closing and digging through. Cheap forearm and hand endurance.
Ring or bar support hold, wrists loaded
Hold yourself at the top of a dip position on rings or a bar, arms locked out, wrists taking compression. Teaches the joint to hold position under load — the same demand as a mantel or a sloper.
Consciously tense the forearm and set the wrist BEFORE you take any load, then grip. The whole point is doing it in the right order until it happens without thinking.

Either one. Squat: bar on the upper back, sit down between the hips keeping the chest up, drive through the whole foot. Trap bar: stand inside the frame, hips back, flat back, stand up. Trap bar is the easier one to learn and the kinder one on the lower back — pick it if you are coming back from zero.

Back foot up on a bench behind you, front foot far enough forward that the front shin stays near vertical. Drop the back knee toward the floor and drive up through the front heel. Brutal, and the single best carryover to running of anything on this list.
Weight in front, soft knees, push the hips back and let the bar travel down the thighs until you feel the hamstrings, then drive the hips forward. The back stays flat throughout.

Knees straight, balls of the feet on a step so the heels can drop below the toes. Rise all the way up, pause, lower slowly. Straight knee means this is gastrocnemius. Add weight — bodyweight stops being a stimulus fast.
Small, fast, springy hops in place off the balls of the feet with the knees almost locked. All the movement is at the ankle. Minimise ground contact time — quiet and quick beats high.

Step off a knee-high box, land on both feet and immediately jump straight back up. The aim is the shortest possible time on the ground, not the biggest jump. Stop the set the moment ground contact starts feeling heavy.

spec.Load: Build to heavy on the straight-knee raise

ex: Knees locked, heels dropped off a step, rise to full height and lower under control. Trains gastrocnemius, which is the calf you can see.

Same movement with the knee bent to about 30 degrees, seated with weight on the thigh or in a half-squat. Bending the knee takes gastrocnemius out and leaves soleus — the muscle that carries most of the load in distance running and the one that quietly feeds achilles trouble.

One leg, heel dropped off a step, raise to full height and lower, repeating until you cannot reach full height any more. Count them. This is a test as much as a set — under about 25 clean reps is a real deficit worth training out.

Heels on the floor with your back against a wall and feet a foot or so out, lift the toes and forefoot toward your shins as high as they go, then lower slowly. This is the front of the shin — the tissue that actually hurts when someone says shin splints.

Foot flat, lift just the big toe while the other four stay down, then reverse it. Then short-foot: pull the ball of the foot toward the heel to raise the arch without curling the toes. Fiddly and worth it.
Two-footed hops staying tall with stiff ankles and quiet landings. Builds the elastic tolerance running actually asks of the achilles.
Weight in front, soft knees, push the hips back and let the bar travel down the thighs until you feel the hamstrings, then drive the hips forward. The back stays flat throughout.
Kneel with your ankles held down, keep the body in one straight line from knee to head, and lower forward as slowly as you can. Catch yourself with your hands. Brutally effective.
On your back, one foot planted, other leg straight or tucked. Drive through the heel and lift the hips, squeezing the glute at the top.
Side plank on the forearm, then lift the top leg toward the ceiling and lower it. Glute medius, which is the actual target when people blame the IT band.
Band around the ankles or just above the knees, step sideways in a half-squat keeping tension on the band. Do not let the knees collapse inward.
Thick band looped behind both knees and anchored in front of you at knee height. Sit back into a squat against the band and hold. Reliably settles kneecap pain rather than provoking it.

spec.Load: Submaximal — pumped but completing all reps
~40% of max — feet stay on the floor
spec.Freq: 3+ ×/week, 6 h clear of hard finger work

ex: All four fingers, knuckles relaxed and open, feet still on the floor. Pull down until you feel a light strain — about 40% of maximum, nowhere near hard.
Index, middle and ring fingers, open hand, feet on the floor taking most of the load.
Index and middle fingers only, open hand, feet down. Two-finger positions load a lot per finger — add them last.
Middle and ring fingers only, open hand, feet down. Usually the strongest of the two-finger pairs.
Index and middle fingers with the middle knuckles bent to 90 degrees, feet down and light.
Middle and ring fingers, knuckles bent to 90 degrees, feet down and light.

spec.Format: V2 → V6 → V2 continuous, no rest
Project at or above the max
20–30 min sustained, or 4–6 min cruise intervals

spec.Recovery: Equal or slightly less than work

spec.Share: 31–48% of weekly volume in build weeks

spec.Work: 45–60 min easy running in the heat
spec.Rule: Consecutive-ish, or it does not stick

ex: Easy run, hottest part of the day
A normal Zone 2 run, deliberately scheduled into the heat rather than around it. Effort stays conversational, which means the PACE will be slower — let it be. The pace is not the point of this run.
Drink to thirst, weigh in and out

Weigh yourself before and after until you know roughly how much you lose per hour, then drink to thirst rather than to a schedule. Both over- and under-drinking are worth avoiding, and thirst is a better guide than a number for a run this length.
Repeat within 14 days of the last block
Heat adaptation fades in two to three weeks. Cluster the exposures rather than scattering them, and re-enter the block rather than treating it as done.

spec.Effort: Fast but smooth — not a sprint

ex: 6 to 8 accelerations of about 20 seconds at a fast but smooth effort, walking back to full recovery between. The aim is relaxation at speed, not a sprint.
Back to the wall, feet up, body stacked and ribs tucked. The easier of the two wall variants and where hold time gets accumulated.
Face the wall and walk the feet up until your chest and hips are close to it. Much harder and much closer to a real freestanding line.
Kick up away from the wall and balance for as long as you can. Correct with the fingers pressing into the floor, not by bending at the hips.
Rings: push-ups on rings, which forces the shoulders to stabilize. Pseudo-planche: hands beside your waist, fingers pointing back, lean forward over the hands.
On your back, lower back pressed flat into the floor, arms and legs extended and lifted just off it. The moment the back arches, the set is over.
The quadruped rocks again but easy and small — this is joint maintenance before bed, not training.
Back foot up on a couch or wall with the knee on the floor, front foot planted ahead. Tuck the pelvis under and stand tall. Hip flexors.
In for 4 seconds, hold 4, out 4, hold 4. Repeat. Slows the nervous system down before sleep.
Continuous easy climbing at a grade you could hold a conversation on. The instant a pump appears the climbing is too hard — drop a grade.
A real break, not a phone break. This is scheduled because the block either side of it does not work without it.
The second continuous 20-minute block, after 5 minutes rest. Expect to drop a grade from the first one to keep the pump away.
Finish by reversing an easy route or problem rather than dropping off. Cheap extra volume and it keeps the footwork honest.
The project. Full rest between burns — 20 minutes minimum, or you are teaching yourself to fail at the crux.
Linked laps — climb, lower, immediately repeat
Climb the route, lower off, and set straight back up it without resting. Two or three laps back to back. This is how a short route buys the time-under-tension of a long one.
Down-climb finish on an easy route
Climb up and reverse it rather than lowering. Cheap extra time on the wall and excellent footwork practice.
The commute run to the gym. Conversational the whole way — walk the steep parts if that is what keeps it easy.
The session as written for that day — this line is just the placeholder it sits in between the two commute runs.
The return leg, on a session-depleted tank. Slower than the way out by default. Eat before you set off.
One end of a barbell in a corner or landmine sleeve, press the other end up and away at an angle. The diagonal path avoids the straight-overhead position that provokes the shoulder.
Push-up on rings, or a bench press lying on the floor so your elbows stop at the ground. Both limit the bottom range that irritates the front of the shoulder.
Chest against an incline bench so the lower back cannot cheat, row the weight to your ribs and squeeze the shoulder blades together.
Cable or band at face height, pull toward your forehead with the elbows high and wide, finishing with the knuckles back. Rear shoulder and mid-back.
Bent forward or chest-supported, arms nearly straight, sweep them out to the sides like opening a book. Light weight.
Face down, lift the arms off the floor tracing a Y, then a T, then a W with the elbows bent. Small range, no weight needed at first.
Roller across the upper back, hands behind the head, extend backwards over it. Keep the ribs down so the movement happens in the upper back, not the lower.
Forearms on a wall, slide them up while pushing into the wall and letting the shoulder blades travel round the ribcage. The push is the exercise.
Stand side-on to a band or cable at chest height, press it straight out in front of you and resist the pull that wants to twist you. Nothing rotates.
Goblet: dumbbell held at the chest, squat down between the knees. Split: one foot forward, one back, drop the back knee toward the floor.
Hand on the head, push the head against it and hold. Front, back, and each side. Nothing moves. Belaying loads the neck and this is what tolerates it.

spec.Rule: Never make up a missed session
spec.Limit: Two missed weeks = re-enter one week back

ex: Missed ONE session — carry on as written
Do nothing. One session does not matter and trying to make it up is how the following week goes wrong.
Missed the key session — move it, drop an easy one
The key session can move within the week. Something easy comes out to make room for it — never stack it on top.
Missed 2–3 days — resume at the current week, skip what was lost
Pick up whatever the plan says for today. No rewinding, no doubling up, no added miles. The week comes out short and that is the correct outcome.
Missed a full week — repeat the last week you completed
Rewind one week rather than jumping to where the calendar says you are. Losing a week costs nothing; jumping into load you have not built costs a season.
Missed 2–3 weeks — drop back one block, rebuild frequency first

Fingers keep most of their strength for 2–4 weeks; the aerobic engine does not, losing roughly 4–7% of VO2max in the first fortnight. So climb close to normal and rebuild running FREQUENCY before mileage, exactly as phase 1 does.

spec.Rule: Test fresh or do not test

ex: Max hang — heaviest 10 s on 20 mm
One 10-second half-crimp hang on a 20 mm edge carrying the most weight you can hold cleanly. Write down the added weight — this is the headline number.
Hang 7 seconds, rest 3 seconds, repeat at bodyweight until the grip gives out. Count the hangs. Same edge and same grip every time or the number means nothing.
The hardest official Kilter benchmark problem you can send in three tries or fewer at 30 degrees. Benchmarks only — setter problems are not comparable between sessions.
First thing, after the toilet, before eating or drinking. Same conditions every time or the trend is noise.

One leg, heel dropped off a step, raise to full height and lower, repeating until you cannot reach full height any more. Count them. This is a test as much as a set — under about 25 clean reps is a real deficit worth training out.
Back squat or trap-bar — heaviest clean 5

The heaviest set of five you can do with clean form and about one rep still in reserve. Same lift and same depth every test or the number means nothing. This is the strength figure the running-economy work should be moving.

pulley.n: Fingers — the injury that ends seasons

spec.Sign: Sharp pain at the base of a finger
spec.Test: Pain resisting flexion at the middle knuckle
spec.Rule: Load it, do not rest it to silence

ex: STOP the session — do not finish the problem
Sharp pain at the base of a finger means the session is over at that instant. Not after this attempt, not after the problem. The single most expensive habit in climbing is one more go.
Days 0–7: pain-free open-hand hangs only, very light
Feet on the ground taking most of your weight, open hand, nowhere near a crimp, and completely pain-free. Loading early is right — loading hard is not.
Weeks 2–6: graded open-hand loading, no crimp
The density-hang protocol at low load is close to the ideal tool here. Open and drag positions only; the crimp stays out.
Weeks 6–12: reintroduce half-crimp at low load
Half-crimp returns before full crimp, and on big edges before small ones. Add one variable at a time.
The last thing to come back, and the thing that caused it. If you rush anything, do not rush this.

spec.Rule: Fall when you are fresh, not when you are pumped

ex: Practice falls, progressively longer, on a warm-up route

Take two or three falls on a bolted route with a clean fall line, starting just above the clip and getting longer. Do them FRESH, early in the session — not for the first time that day when you are pumped and frightened.
Name the feeling out loud before the redpoint burn
Say what you are actually feeling before you set off — nervous, excited, tired. Naming it is the emotional-regulation half, and that is the half fall practice alone does not train.
Breathe out slowly at the clip before the crux
One long exhale at the last good stance. Slows the heart rate and stops the over-gripping that turns a crux into a fall.
Commit to the move, not to the clip
Climb to the next good position rather than clip-to-clip. Lunging for a draw from a bad stance is what most 5.12 falls are actually made of.
Rehearse the sequence with eyes closed on the ground
Two minutes before the burn, run the whole sequence in your head with your eyes shut — hands, feet, where you breathe, where you shake out.
Tall but easy problems, well within your limit. If down-climbing it would not feel comfortable, do not top it out.
Reverse the problem instead of walking off. Doubles the movement volume and is the habit that keeps highballing sane.
Four to six problems climbing gradually up in difficulty, stopping well short of anything hard. The bridge between warm-up and project burns.
Full-effort attempts on the two or three problems you came for. Five or more minutes between burns — outdoor sessions fail from impatience far more often than from weakness.
Two or three easy problems to finish, moving smoothly. Ends the session on good movement rather than on a failed attempt.
Full-effort attempts on the route you are trying to send, with at least 20 minutes between them.
Volume pitches below your limit. The point is time on rock and tactics — resting on the route, clipping stances, reading sequences.
Genuinely sit down. Twenty minutes between redpoint attempts, five or more between boulder burns. Short rests turn a session into practising failure.
Weighted explosive pull-up, hands leave the bar
Pull hard enough and fast enough that your hands actually come off the bar at the top. Add weight only while that stays true — if the hands stop leaving, the weight is too heavy for what this trains.
Pull up with both arms, let go with one, and lower on the single arm over 5 seconds. Turns your one-arm pull-up into a one-arm lock-off, which is the position a hard dyno catches in.
Pull to the chest, then roll the wrists and drive the elbows back to get above the rings, and press out. The transition is the whole skill.
Same movement on a fixed bar, which is less forgiving on the shoulder than rings because the hands cannot rotate.

spec.Goal: Press-out from a deep, high-elbow position

ex: Hands on a waist-high box or volume, press down and bring the body up over the hands from a deep position with the elbows high. This is the Midnight Lightning topout, not a dip.
The same press-out with only one hand on the box. Slow and controlled.
Find the deepest part of the mantel press that is completely pain-free and hold there. Builds strength at the exact angle that fails.
A dip on rings, but only lowering to a depth that stays pain-free. Rings let the shoulder rotate naturally, which a fixed bar forbids. Lower the floor by an inch at a time over months.
Locked out at the top of the rings, arms straight, rings turned slightly out. Hold still — the shaking is the exercise.
From the ring support position, lower yourself over a full 5 seconds. Builds tolerance to shear load at the bottom of the mantel position.
Fingers and thumb inside a rubber band, open the hand against it. Strengthens the extensors, which balances the enormous flexor load climbing puts through the pulleys.
Forearm resting on your thigh, palm down, light dumbbell in hand. Lift the back of the hand up, lower it slowly.
Same position, palm up. Curl the weight toward you, lower it slowly.
Hold a hammer or wrench near the end of the handle, elbow tucked at 90 degrees, and rotate the palm up then down. The long handle is what makes it hard.
Hand flat on a table, lift one finger at a time as high as it will go while the others stay down. Slow and deliberate.

spec.Duration: 5 min, plus the 3 min wrist dose = 8
spec.Days: Work days and early crag starts

ex: Sit tall, straighten one knee and pull the toes toward you while tucking the chin, then bend the knee and look up. Glide back and forth — this mobilizes the nerve WITHOUT the sustained hamstring stretch that sets your knees off.
Sitting with both knees bent at 90 degrees, one leg in front and one out to the side, rotate both knees across to the other side without using your hands.
Sit still and put attention on the breath. When the mind wanders, bring it back. That returning is the practice.
Consciously tense the forearm and set the wrist BEFORE you take any load, then grip. The whole point is doing it in the right order until it happens without thinking.
All three of the above back to back — fingers forward, fingers back, then fingers out to the sides. 30 seconds each.

Sit tall, straighten one knee and pull the toes toward you while tucking the chin, then bend the knee and look up. Glide back and forth — this mobilizes the nerve WITHOUT the sustained hamstring stretch that sets your knees off.
Sitting with both knees bent at 90 degrees, one leg in front and one out to the side, rotate both knees across to the other side without using your hands.
Back foot up on a couch or wall with the knee on the floor, front foot planted ahead. Tuck the pelvis under and stand tall. Hip flexors.
Lie on your side, knees bent and stacked, arms out in front. Open the top arm across your body like a book cover and follow it with your eyes. Rotation comes from the upper back.
On all fours, slide one arm underneath your body and across, letting the shoulder and upper back rotate down toward the floor.
Foot a few inches from a wall, drive the knee forward over the toes to touch the wall without the heel lifting. Move the foot back as it improves.
Either follow the breath, or move attention slowly through the body from feet to head noticing what is there.
10 to 15 g of hydrolyzed collagen or gelatin with 50 mg or more of vitamin C, taken about an hour before loading so the amino acids are circulating when the tissue is loaded.
Slow isometric hangs or block lifts
Either a light hang or a pinch-block lift off the floor. Take 3 to 5 seconds to build to full tension, hold, then release just as slowly. Search "no-hang block lift".
The point is the ramp, not the load: build force over 3 to 5 seconds, hold, release over 3 to 5 seconds. Snatching onto the edge is the thing this drill exists to stop.
